title: The Bobo Doll (Bandura, 1961)

youtube.title: A Child Watched an Adult Hit a Clown. Then This Happened #Shorts
youtube.description:
You're a small child. Across the room, an adult is punching a giant inflatable clown.
Then you're left in a room full of toys, with the same clown.

This is Albert Bandura's 1961 Bobo doll experiment, told from the inside. Children who watched the attack copied it, often the exact punches and the exact words. Nobody rewarded them and nobody told them to hit: they learned it just by watching.

Who is watching YOU, and what are they learning? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Bandura, A., Ross, D., & Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575-582.
- Bandura, A. (1977). Social Learning Theory. Prentice Hall.

#psychology #bandura #bobodoll #sociallearning #shorts

sources: Bandura, Ross & Ross (1961), J Abnormal & Social Psychology 63(3): 72 children (36 boys, 36 girls) aged about 3 to 6 (37-69 months) from the Stanford University nursery school.

Same paper: the aggressive adult model sat on the Bobo doll, punched it in the nose, hit it on the head with a mallet, tossed and kicked it, and said things like 'Sock him in the nose' and 'Pow'; the child meanwhile worked on a picture/sticker activity in another corner of the room.

Same paper: afterwards each child was mildly frustrated, then left in a room with toys including a mallet and a smaller Bobo doll, observed through a one-way mirror; children who had seen the aggressive model reproduced many of its exact physical and verbal acts, while children who saw a non-aggressive model or no model showed much less imitative aggression. No rewards or instructions to imitate were given.
lines: You're a small child. An adult is punching a giant inflatable clown. And you are watching every move.
Nineteen sixty-one, Stanford. You play with stickers at a little table. Across the room, an adult starts beating the clown.
They sit on it. They punch its nose. They hit its head with a mallet and shout: sock him!
Then you're taken to a room full of toys. And there, in the corner, stands the same clown.
Nobody tells you what to do. A researcher watches quietly behind a mirror. You pick up the mallet.
Seventy-two children took part. The ones who saw the attack copied it, often the exact punches and the exact words.
Children who saw a calm adult, or no adult at all, were far less aggressive.
Nobody rewarded them. Nobody told them to hit. They learned it just by watching.
So the people around you aren't just acting. They're teaching. Who is watching you, and what are they learning?
